OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: OIIX/Tehran FIR remains only partially open. The eastern part is available for overflights, while the western part remains closed, and very few international operators are using Iranian airspace. Multiple states now advise their operators not to enter the FIR. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is misidentification of civil aircraft by Iranian air-defence systems during heightened military tension. Iran remains on high military alert, while missile activity, air-defence operations and the risk of sudden escalation create a high risk at all altitudes. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 shows how quickly this can affect civil aviation. France, Germany, Italy, the UK, Canada and the US all advise against, or prohibit, ops in OIIX/Tehran FIR. Major events: Sep 2026: France, Germany and Italy issued or renewed warnings advising their operators not to enter OIIX/Tehran FIR. Jun 2026: Iran partially reopened the eastern part of OIIX/Tehran FIR for overflights, while the western part remained closed. Mar 2026: OIIX/Tehran FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation. Jun 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran exchanged missile attacks, leading to widespread airspace avoidance. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying the aircraft as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: The US and coalition military mission in Iraq ended on Sep 30, with forces departing Erbil. Iraqi airspace remains open to overflights, but the withdrawal removes a layer of US air defence around ORER/Erbil while armed factions remain active. This leaves Iraq more exposed to missile and drone attacks and localised insecurity, particularly in the Kurdistan Region. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk remains missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts, alongside the potential for misidentification by air defence systems and the presence of armed groups with access to anti-aircraft weapons. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude. Despite the FIR remaining open, most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Major events: Oct 2026: US and coalition forces leave Erbil, removing a layer of air defence as armed factions remain active. Mar 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR closed following strikes on Iran and Iranian retaliation. Jun 2025: Airspace closed after Israeli strikes on Iran, missiles and drones transited Iraq. Apr 2024: Airspace closed during Iran's drone and missile attack on Israel. Apr 2023: Drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under revised FAA rules.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: Lebanese airspace (the OLBB/Beirut FIR) remains high risk, with Israeli military activity continuing despite ceasefire efforts. Most international operators continue to avoid the airspace. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict, including Israeli airstrikes and the risk of misidentification by air defence systems. Several countries advise operators to avoid Lebanese airspace. EASA maintains this advice at all altitudes, except for flights to and from Beirut that approach from the sea or depart over the sea. GPS jamming and spoofing are also reported in the FIR. Major events: Oct 2026: EASA maintains its warning against Lebanese airspace, with exceptions for Beirut flights over the sea. Sep 2026: Germany, Italy, France and the UK maintain airspace warnings for Lebanon. Aug 2026: Lebanon warns of increased GPS jamming and spoofing, recommending conventional ATS routes. Feb - July 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued despite ceasefire extensions. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS jamming and spoofing reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: OJAC/Amman FIR remains open and Jordan has not published conflict-related airspace restrictions. However, the security situation deteriorated after renewed attacks in early September, and current international guidance is to avoid the FIR at all altitudes. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts. Jordan has previously been affected by missiles and drones crossing its airspace during escalations involving Israel and Iran. Air-defence activity adds a risk of interception, misidentification and falling debris. France and Germany advise not to enter the FIR, while European guidance also recommends avoiding it at all altitudes. Major events: Sep 2026: Renewed attacks in early September increased the risk to civil aviation in Jordanian airspace. France subsequently renewed its warning for French operators not to enter OJAC/Amman FIR. Aug 2026: Germany advised its operators not to enter OJAC/Amman FIR. Feb-Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during Iran’s drone and missile attack on Israel.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response.

cross.detail: Sep 2026: Kuwait has kept restrictions on the OKAC/Kuwait FIR in place following the wider US-Iran conflict. The airspace is open for approved flights to OKKK/Kuwait airport, but overflights remain prohibited. The restriction has now been extended into November. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk remains missile and drone activity linked to the wider regional conflict. Kuwait has already been directly affected by Iranian attacks, including strikes on OKKK/Kuwait airport where Terminal 1 was damaged in June. Military activity around the Kuwait/Bahrain FIR boundary has also been reported. GPS interference, ATC congestion and reroutes remain wider operational issues across the region. Major events: Sep 2026: Kuwait extended its airspace restrictions, with overflights still prohibited and approved arrivals/departures permitted. Aug 2026: EASA issued revised guidance for the Persian Gulf following the US-Iran conflict, identifying continued risks from missile and drone activity, air defence operations and military activity. Feb-July 2026: OKAC/Kuwait FIR was closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR remains open, but the risk picture is still elevated following the US-Iran conflict and military activity around the Strait of Hormuz. Some restrictions remain in place over the FIR’s waters, while short-notice disruption remains possible. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to the wider regional conflict. Bahrain hosts major US military facilities and could be directly exposed to Iranian attacks. Air-defence activity also creates a risk of misidentification, falling debris and sudden airspace restrictions. Ops over the Persian Gulf waters within OBBB/Bahrain FIR should be avoided except for necessary arrivals and departures, while France advises to exercise great caution throughout the FIR. Major events: Sep 2026: France renewed its warning for French operators to exercise great caution in OBBB/Bahrain FIR. Jul-Sep 2026: A Persian Gulf airspace advisory was issued and later revised following renewed military activity. It now advises avoiding the waters within OBBB/Bahrain FIR except for necessary arrivals and departures. Feb-Jul 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. Mar 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks affected several Gulf states, including airspace around Bahrain.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR remains open, but the risk picture is still elevated following the US-Iran conflict and continuing military activity in the Persian Gulf. Some restrictions remain in place over the FIR’s waters, while short-notice disruption remains possible. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to the wider regional conflict. Qatar hosts major US military facilities and could be directly exposed to Iranian attacks. Air-defence activity also creates a risk of misidentification, falling debris and sudden airspace restrictions. EASA advises avoiding the Persian Gulf waters within OTDF/Doha FIR except for necessary arrivals and departures, while France advises great caution throughout the FIR. Major events: Sep 2026: France renewed its warning for French operators to exercise great caution in OTDF/Doha FIR. Jul-Sep 2026: A Persian Gulf airspace advisory was issued and later revised following renewed military activity. It now advises avoiding the waters within OTDF/Doha FIR except for necessary arrivals and departures. Feb-Jul 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. Mar 2026: An Iranian missile strike was reported near Al Udeid Air Base, close to Doha.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: OOMM/Muscat FIR remains open and is a key part of the main southern bypass route around the Middle East conflict zone. The risk remains elevated due to military activity around the Strait of Hormuz. Ops over the Gulf of Oman within the FIR west of 58°E should be avoided. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is military activity around the Strait of Hormuz. Oman sits close to the strait and remains an important link in the Egypt-Saudi-Oman routing used by many operators. Ops over the Gulf of Oman within OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E should be avoided. France advises to exercise great caution throughout the FIR. Major events: Sep 2026: France renewed its warning for French operators to exercise great caution in OOMM/Muscat FIR. Jul-Sep 2026: A Persian Gulf airspace advisory was issued and later revised following renewed military activity. It continues to advise avoiding the Gulf of Oman within OOMM west of 58°E. Feb-Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the southern bypass route. Jun 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran exchanged missile attacks, leading to widespread airspace avoidance.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: Syrian airspace (the OSTT/Damascus FIR) remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it again as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. EASA has eased its advice, now allowing flights at FL260 and above in most of the FIR, although restrictions remain in the western part of the airspace. The primary risk is military activity in and around Syrian airspace, including Israeli airstrikes and the interception of missiles and drones. Falling debris from intercepted weapons can pose a risk to civil aircraft, while air defence systems also create a risk of misidentification. Drones, rockets and MANPADS are an additional threat at lower levels. Major events: Oct 2026: EASA eased its Syria CZIB, allowing FL260+ in most of the Damascus FIR. Oct 2026: Regional operators increasingly using Syrian airspace as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. March 2026: OSTT/Damascus FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo. Feb 2020: A320 diverted after being caught in crossfire near Damascus. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: Yemen remains an active conflict zone, and the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (the OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can still use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions of Yemeni airspace. The security situation has deteriorated sharply since Sep 2026, with renewed fighting between Houthi and Saudi-backed government forces and an increase in missile and drone attacks. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also carry risks. The primary risk is intentional targeting by Houthi forces and other groups with access to sophisticated missiles, drones and anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft are also exposed to the wider military activity, including Saudi-led airstrikes and Houthi missile and drone attacks. Major events: Oct 2026: Fighting has intensified between Houthi and Saudi-backed government forces, particularly around the Bab el-Mandeb area. Oct 2026: OYAA/Aden airport was targeted - a missile landed near the runway as a Cairo flight was approaching and the flight was diverted to Jeddah. Jul 2026: Yemeni government forces struck the runway at OYSN/Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport remains closed following Israeli airstrikes. Jan 2024: US and UK airstrikes against Houthi targets began following missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: Drone attacks continue across Russia. On 6 October, Moscow reported more than 650 Ukrainian drones targeting the capital region, most of them intercepted. Most operators avoid Russian airspace. Those still flying there should expect short-notice closures or reroutes, including during the day. Ukraine’s airspace remains closed to civil aviation, and restrictions remain in place in Russian airspace near the border. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Ukraine and Russia Update March 2022 The primary risk is that civil aircraft could be misidentified or caught in air-defence activity as Russia responds to Ukrainian drones and missiles. EASA advises operators within its scope to avoid Russian airspace west of 60°E at all altitudes. Several countries also restrict flights near the Ukraine border, and GNSS interference adds to the risk. Major events: Oct 2026: More than 650 Ukrainian drones reportedly targeted the Moscow region. Most were intercepted, and air-defence activity added to the risk for civil flights. Jul 2026: EASA extended its recommendation to avoid Russian airspace west of 60°E. Dec 2024: Azerbaijan Airlines Flight 8243 was shot down near URMG/Grozny during Russian air-defence activity. EASA cites the incident as an example of the risk of misidentification. Jul 2023 - ongoing: Drone strikes around Moscow have triggered air-defence activity and repeated temporary airport closures. Feb 2022: Russia invaded Ukraine. Ukraine’s airspace closed to civil aviation, and several countries restricted their operators near the Russia-Ukraine border.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. There is an ongoing active conflict in Ukraine between Russian and Ukrainian forces. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near to their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All the major countries who regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have since issued total flight bans for Ukraine due to risk from military activity at all levels. (Several other countries have also issued flight bans for Ukraine but we have not listed them all here due to sheer volume). The primary risk is an unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752), or confusion. The secondary risk is potential lack of Ukrainian Air Traffic Control Service at short notice (Cyber Attack), and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments for civil aircraft. OPSGROUP article: Ukraine and Russia Update March 2022 Prior to February 2022, there were two areas of concern in Ukraine - the conflict in the far east of the country (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the double claim over ATC and airspace in Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. There is ongoing fighting in Sudan between government and militant forces. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no Notams are being issued. There is a Contingency Plan available with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan. If routing via nearby airspace, be aware of other active warnings in close proximity. Several countries have issued airspace warning advising their operators not to enter the airspace of Sudan, due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. OPSGROUP article: Sudan Airspace Update, Nov 2025 The primary risk now relates to security on the ground for any unplanned diversions to airports in Sudan. Throughout the conflict, there have been reports of passenger jets being targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport. The secondary risk relates to Sudan’s proximity to South Sudan - which has poor levels of ATC provision for overflights below FL245. Major events : Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft was shot down by local militia over North Darfur (Western Sudan, near the border with Chad). Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15. Sudan’s airspace closed, South Sudan’s airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25. HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days, with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Some progress made in Oct 2020 with the formation of a new government, but Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between various rival militia groups across the country. There is a high risk to civil aircraft. Libyan airspace (HLLL/Tripoli FIR) should be avoided entirely. Total flight ban for US operators, and several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is a misident by Libyan air defense systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya, including HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity reported over the high-seas which is either operating as OAT or not in control with ATC. Risk remains high across Libya at all flight levels, and avoidance of all airspace and airports is strongly recommended. The secondary risk is that reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed. The past few years have seen regular ATS and radar outages across the HLLL FIR airspace, and severe limitations in VHF capability, with operators having to communicate with Malta ATC for guidance. Libya Airspace Update, Feb 2024 (OPSGROUP article) Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. Tripoli mass evacuation of aircraft (OPSGROUP article) July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aircraft are no longer banned from Italian airports and airspace if they want to fly from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air defense forces claimed to have shot down a US drone operating in the vicinity of Benghazi during a period of increased tensions and threats of renewed violence between competing militias vying for control of Tripoli. June 2022: Failed attempt by militia to enter Tripoli to seize control of government offices, resulting in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Videos on social media showing planes landing at the airport as shells are falling in the background. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on the capital, Tripoli, declared a no-fly-zone around the city, threatening to shoot-down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias destroyed most of the airport's facilities. The airport remains closed to this day; most flights operate out of HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution in Mali airspace at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state run paramilitary force operating anti aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. The primary risks include MANPADS and other surface to air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low level and airport phase operations carry the highest exposure. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs. They have a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. More info can be found in this ASECNA AIP SUP. Major events : April 2026: The security situation has escalated sharply. On April 25, multiple armed groups carried out coordinated attacks nationwide against state and military targets, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako. Sporadic fighting is ongoing. France has issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS, or use it as an alternate. Several other states maintain active airspace warnings due to risk of anti-aircraft fire and terrorist activity. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire. Multiple attacks occurred across the city and the airport closed temporarily. This was the first major attack in Bamako in several years. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali due to escalating militant activity. Commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu were cancelled after shelling near the airport. A military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao the same day, with reports it may have been shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup. Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali.

cross.detail: The situation on the ground is highly unstable and there is an inherent risk to civilians and aircraft. The central government has little control of the major cities and ports, with ongoing attacks from extremist militants targeting civilians who continue to show an intent to target aviation interests. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at the lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across Somalia’s airspace (the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR) below FL260 except for flights transiting the overwater portion of the airspace going to/from HDAM/Djibouti airport across the border in Ethiopia. Several other countries have issued airspace warnings advising against operating below FL260. The secondary risk is from aircraft transiting Somalia being contacted by unauthorized ATC units, who have been issuing climb/descent instructions that conflict with the official ones issued by Mogadishu Control. There’s also an authority dispute in the north of the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR. From Nov 2025, Somaliland has said all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR. Expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events : Feb 2024: OPSGROUP received several reports of aircraft within the Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a ‘fake controller’ on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. More info here. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled operations including combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) not reporting position, altitude or routing, Oct 2022: The Somalian government issued a warning that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups amid the escalating conflict in the country. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. More info here. 2020-ongoing: Multiple instances of Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down while on approach to Bardale airstrip , killing all six people on board - an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces stationed in the region to combat Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: The OPKR/Karachi FIR and OPLR/Lahore FIR remain open to international traffic, but Indian-registered aircraft and Indian operators are still barred. The ceasefire between India and Pakistan has largely held since May 2025, but the situation remains fragile and military activity could resume with little warning. Separately, tensions along the Afghanistan border have risen again. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Pakistan/India Airspace Update - 2025 The primary risk is militant activity and anti-aircraft weapons, including missiles that can be fired from the ground, especially at lower altitudes in western Pakistan. In Kashmir, renewed fighting between India and Pakistan could put aircraft at risk of being mistaken for military targets. EASA advises against flights below FL260 over Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. France, Germany and Italy also advise caution at lower altitudes in the OPKR/Karachi FIR and OPLR/Lahore FIR. Major events: Oct 2026: Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan’s Kunar and Helmand provinces renewed cross-border fighting. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated, but no new airspace closures or overflight bans were issued. Commercial traffic continued through the OAKX/Kabul FIR, including on routes P500 and G500. May 2025: India and Pakistan exchanged strikes and shelling in Kashmir. A ceasefire followed, but both countries continue to bar each other’s aircraft. Jan 2024: Iran carried out missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Pilots reported GPS spoofing around the OPLR/Lahore FIR, particularly near OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights after major clashes with India.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: The OPKR/Karachi FIR and OPLR/Lahore FIR remain open to international traffic, but Indian-registered aircraft and Indian operators are still barred. The ceasefire between India and Pakistan has largely held since May 2025, but the situation remains fragile and military activity could resume with little warning. Separately, tensions along the Afghanistan border have risen again. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Pakistan/India Airspace Update - 2025 The primary risk is militant activity and anti-aircraft weapons, including missiles that can be fired from the ground, especially at lower altitudes in western Pakistan. In Kashmir, renewed fighting between India and Pakistan could put aircraft at risk of being mistaken for military targets. EASA advises against flights below FL260 over Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. France, Germany and Italy also advise caution at lower altitudes in the OPKR/Karachi FIR and OPLR/Lahore FIR. Major events: Oct 2026: Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan’s Kunar and Helmand provinces renewed cross-border fighting. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated, but no new airspace closures or overflight bans were issued. Commercial traffic continued through the OAKX/Kabul FIR, including on routes P500 and G500. May 2025: India and Pakistan exchanged strikes and shelling in Kashmir. A ceasefire followed, but both countries continue to bar each other’s aircraft. Jan 2024: Iran carried out missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Pilots reported GPS spoofing around the OPLR/Lahore FIR, particularly near OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights after major clashes with India.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances.

cross.detail: Oct 2026: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains open and uncontrolled, with no ATC service. It continues to carry Europe-Asia traffic rerouted around Middle East restrictions. Renewed Pakistani airstrikes have raised the risk near the border. See OPSGROUP Briefing : March 2026 - Afghanistan Overflight Update. The primary risk comes from military activity near the Pakistan border and the lack of ATC across the OAKX/Kabul FIR. EASA, France, Germany and Canada advise against ops below FL320. Italy’s restriction allows P500 and G500 below its 25,000 ft AGL limit, while US operators may use those routes from FL300. With no ATC, aircraft must follow published contingency routes and use TIBA procedures to maintain separation. Major events: Oct 2026: Pakistani airstrikes in Kunar and Helmand renewed cross-border fighting. The UN reported civilian casualties, while Pakistan said it had targeted militants. March 2026: Middle East airspace closures sent more Europe-Asia traffic through the OAKX/Kabul FIR. Cross-border fighting with Pakistan also resumed. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: After the Taliban takeover and allied withdrawal, the OAKX/Kabul FIR lost ATC service and became uncontrolled Class G airspace.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Oct 2026: Government-aligned forces have retaken Mekelle after Tigrayan forces withdrew from the city on 3 October. Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to HAMK/Mekelle on 11 October, but fighting and wider tensions in northern Ethiopia continue. The primary risk is armed conflict, including drone, artillery and anti-aircraft activity, particularly in Tigray, Afar and Amhara. The UK advises operators to consider the risk when overflying these regions. Italy and Germany warn of military threats across the HAAA/Addis Ababa FIR. EASA advises risk assessment below FL260, especially north of 8.5°N. French operators should remain at or above FL320 in specified northern airspace and use great caution below FL320 elsewhere in the FIR. Major Events: Oct 2026: Government-aligned forces retook Mekelle. Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to HAMK/Mekelle on 11 Oct. Fighting and regional tensions continue. Sep 2026: Tigrayan forces took control of HAMK/Mekelle. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to HAMK/Mekelle, HATF/Axum and HASI/Shire as fighting escalated. Feb 2024: Fighting flared again in Amhara, including air strikes. Nov 2022: A peace deal was agreed in Tigray. Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekelle. July 2021: HAAA/Addis Ababa FIR airspace below FL290 was closed over Tigray after a military aircraft was reportedly shot down near Mekelle. Nov 2020: Conflict escalated in Tigray. Airways were closed, airports hit by rockets and missiles fired into Eritrea. Sep 2018: Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike. Retired and foreign controllers were brought in to cover ops.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021. There is conflict and violence across many parts of the country, involving air strikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at the lower flight levels due to the potential risk from military ops, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. We have also had reports of GPS jamming (and maybe spoofing) in the north of the FIR for overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events : Feb 2026: Armed groups targeted an ATR with passengers on board preparing to depart VYMK/Myitkyina with a first-person view suicide drone. Damage was caused to the nose, midesection and tail and was later declared a war crime under the Geneva Convention. The airport was temporarily closed. Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin, which borders China. They likely used a man portable air defence system (MANPAD). Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups against military targets across the country, including a makeshift drone which dropped bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 over the mainland in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: Myanmar’s main airport VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following attack by resistance groups with improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of the ATR 72 aircraft on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government. ATC strike at the end of Feb resulted in no ATC service provided to overflights (read more on that here ). Since then, there have been increasing strikes and mass protests by opposition activists,  as well as clashes with militia and airstrikes on areas where militia are known to be active.
